title: A Buffer That Breathes
endLine: Blood's buffer works far from its pKa because breathing removes CO₂.

scenes.tts: Water lets weak bonds add up to a fold. But ionic attractions need charges, and p H decides which groups carry them. Blood holds its p H in a window a tenth of a unit wide. By the usual rule, its buffer is poor. How does it hold?
scenes.caption: Water lets weak bonds add up to a fold. But ionic attractions need charges, and pH decides which groups carry them. Blood holds its pH in a window a tenth of a unit wide. By the usual rule, its buffer is poor. How does it hold?
scenes.narration: Water lets weak bonds add up to a fold. But ionic attractions need charges, and pH decides which groups carry them. Blood holds its pH in a window a tenth of a unit wide. By the usual rule, its buffer is poor. How does it hold?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, continued from the first film without a reset: the cross-section of a glass of water fills the frame (x -6.4..6.4, y -3.4..3.4), thin BLUE outline, about 140 small BLUE dots drifting by the same Brownian updater for the whole film. COLOR MAP, carried: BLUE water, GREEN polar beads, YELLOW oily blobs, GOLD totals, gauges and the take-home. NEW in this film: ORANGE small dots = protons (H+); WHITE discs = the form holding its proton (HA), and later WHITE bubbles = dissolved CO₂ (the acid side); PURPLE discs = the form that has let go (A-), and later PURPLE = bicarbonate. No molecular structures anywhere: beads, blobs, dots, discs, bars. Labels size 30 or larger, full opacity, at most 5 words, at most 6 labelled things on screen. OPEN on the first film's folded ball (YELLOW blobs inside, GREEN beads outside) in the middle of the glass, already gently breathing. On 'add up to a fold', thin GREEN links flicker between surface beads. On 'need charges', two surface GREEN beads gain small '+' and '-' tags and a GREEN link snaps between them. On 'p H decides', an ORANGE proton dot lands on the '-' bead and the tag vanishes; the link between the pair goes slack, then the proton lifts off and the link snaps back. On 'Blood holds', the ball shrinks to a small corner icon (top left) and a tall vertical GOLD gauge rises on the right edge, labelled 'blood pH', scale 6.0 to 7.6 with ticks every 0.2; a narrow GOLD band from 7.35 to 7.45 glows, labelled 'the window'. A WHITE needle sits at 7.40 and trembles slightly inside the band. On 'its buffer is poor', a chip 'poor buffer?' (GOLD, 32) drops in beside the gauge. On 'how does it hold?', a large GOLD '?' pulses beside the needle.

Title 'A Buffer That Breathes' (GOLD, 44) fades in across the top for 2 s while the '?' and the chip fade out. The BLUE water dots keep drifting; the needle keeps trembling at 7.40 in the window. The folded-ball icon fades out.

scenes.tts: Take a group that can hold a proton. Below its p K a, it mostly keeps it. Above, it mostly lets go. At the p K a, half and half.
scenes.caption: Take a group that can hold a proton. Below its pKa, it mostly keeps it. Above, it mostly lets go. At the pKa, half and half.
scenes.narration: Take a group that can hold a proton. Below its pKa, it mostly keeps it. Above, it mostly lets go. At the pKa, half and half.
scenes.visual: The blood gauge slides to a small inset at the right edge (still visible, needle at 7.40). In the middle of the glass, a 10 x 10 grid of 100 discs appears, filling about 60% of the frame height. Under the grid, a horizontal slider labelled 'pH − pKa' runs from -2 to +2, ticks at each whole number, with a GOLD knob. On 'Below', the knob sits at -2: 99 discs are WHITE, each with an ORANGE proton dot on it, and 1 is PURPLE. On 'Above', the knob slides to +2: ORANGE dots lift off into the water and drift away as discs turn PURPLE, until 99 are PURPLE and 1 is WHITE. On 'half and half', the knob slides back to 0 and the grid settles at exactly 50 WHITE (with protons) and 50 PURPLE, labelled 'at the pKa: 50%'. Disc counts follow the lesson's table; nothing in between is shown as a number.

scenes.tts: Each p H unit past the p K a shifts the ratio tenfold. One unit above, about ninety-one percent have let go. Two units, about ninety-nine. One p H unit is worth about one weak bond.
scenes.caption: Each pH unit past the pKa shifts the ratio tenfold. One unit above, about 91% have let go. Two units, about 99. One pH unit is worth about one weak bond.
scenes.narration: Each pH unit past the pKa shifts the ratio tenfold. One unit above, about 91% have let go. Two units, about 99. One pH unit is worth about one weak bond.
scenes.visual: Same grid and slider. On 'tenfold', the knob steps from 0 to +1: discs flip from WHITE to PURPLE (protons lifting off) until 91 PURPLE and 9 WHITE remain; a GOLD tag above the grid reads '10 : 1'. On 'Two units', the knob steps to +2: 99 PURPLE, 1 WHITE; the tag morphs to '100 : 1'. Counts are from the lesson's table (91% and 99%). On 'worth about one weak bond', a GOLD chip slides in from the left edge, styled like the first film's ledger rows: '1 pH unit ≈ 5.9 kJ/mol'. Beside it a short GREEN link between two beads pulses once, labelled 'one weak bond'.

scenes.tts: Near the p K a, both forms are plentiful, ready to absorb acid or base. Far away, one form has nearly run out. So a sealed flask buffers best within about one unit.
scenes.caption: Near the pKa, both forms are plentiful, ready to absorb acid or base. Far away, one form has nearly run out. So a sealed flask buffers best within about one unit.
scenes.narration: Near the pKa, both forms are plentiful, ready to absorb acid or base. Far away, one form has nearly run out. So a sealed flask buffers best within about one unit.
scenes.visual: The ledger chip and GREEN link fade. The knob returns to 0 (50 WHITE, 50 PURPLE). On 'ready to absorb', a few ORANGE proton dots rain in from the top; each lands on a PURPLE disc, which turns WHITE, while a few WHITE discs lose their dots and turn PURPLE to show base; the grid stays near half and half. On 'Far away', the knob slides to -2: 99 WHITE, 1 PURPLE; the same ORANGE rain falls, the lone PURPLE disc takes one proton and turns WHITE, and the extra ORANGE dots pile up loose in the water. On 'sealed flask', the glass outline gains a GOLD lid that clicks shut on top, labelled 'sealed flask'. A GOLD bracket spans -1 to +1 on the slider, labelled 'works best'.

scenes.tts: Blood's buffer is bicarbonate, with carbon dioxide as the acid side. Its effective p K a is six point one. Blood sits at seven point four, one point three off. About twenty bicarbonates per carbon dioxide.
scenes.caption: Blood's buffer is bicarbonate, with CO₂ as the acid side. Its effective pKa is 6.1. Blood sits at 7.4, 1.3 off. About 20 bicarbonates per CO₂.
scenes.narration: Blood's buffer is bicarbonate, with CO₂ as the acid side. Its effective pKa is 6.1. Blood sits at 7.4, 1.3 off. About 20 bicarbonates per CO₂.
scenes.visual: The 100-disc grid and slider dissolve. The glass keeps its GOLD lid. Inside the glass, two vertical bars rise from a shared baseline, side by side, on a hidden scale 0 to 25 millimolar (bar height proportional to millimolar): a PURPLE bar labelled 'bicarbonate' and a WHITE bar labelled 'CO₂', with WHITE bubbles drifting up inside the WHITE bar. The blood gauge grows back to full size on the right edge, needle at 7.40 in the GOLD window. On 'six point one', a GOLD tick at 6.1 on the gauge lights, labelled 'pKa 6.1'. On 'one point three off', a GOLD bracket spans 6.1 to 7.4 on the gauge, labelled '1.3 units'. On 'twenty', the bars settle at 24 (PURPLE) and 1.2 (WHITE); the WHITE bar is a short stub. A GOLD tag between them reads '20 : 1'.

scenes.tts: Take twenty-four millimolar bicarbonate and one point two millimolar carbon dioxide. Seal the flask and add ten millimolar strong acid. Each millimolar turns one bicarbonate into carbon dioxide.
scenes.caption: Take 24 mM bicarbonate and 1.2 mM CO₂. Seal the flask and add 10 mM strong acid. Each mM turns one bicarbonate into CO₂.
scenes.narration: Take 24 mM bicarbonate and 1.2 mM CO₂. Seal the flask and add 10 mM strong acid. Each mM turns one bicarbonate into CO₂.
scenes.visual: The bars get number tags: '24 mM' on the PURPLE bar, '1.2 mM' on the WHITE bar. The GOLD lid is shut. On 'add ten millimolar', a cloud of ORANGE proton dots pours in through a small funnel at the top edge, labelled '+10 mM acid'. On 'turns one bicarbonate', ORANGE dots meet the top of the PURPLE bar; each meeting turns a slice of PURPLE into a WHITE bubble that floats over to the WHITE bar. Motion only in this scene: the bars begin to change but have not yet reached their final heights.

scenes.tts: Bicarbonate falls to fourteen. Carbon dioxide piles up to eleven point two. The ratio collapses to barely above one. The p H drops to about six point two.
scenes.caption: Bicarbonate falls to 14. CO₂ piles up to 11.2. The ratio collapses to barely above one. The pH drops to about 6.2.
scenes.narration: Bicarbonate falls to 14. CO₂ piles up to 11.2. The ratio collapses to barely above one. The pH drops to about 6.2.
scenes.visual: Computed from the lesson's numbers: the PURPLE bar shrinks from 24 to 14 (tag '14 mM'); the WHITE bar grows from 1.2 to 11.2 (tag '11.2 mM'), its bubbles pressing against the shut GOLD lid. The ratio tag morphs '20 : 1' to '1.25 : 1'. On 'drops', the gauge needle slides from 7.40 down to 6.20 (6.1 + log10(14/11.2) = 6.197), leaving the GOLD window far above; the needle turns dim and a tag 'sealed: about 6.2' appears beside it. Hold the result.

scenes.tts: Now open the flask. Breathing carries the extra carbon dioxide away, holding it at one point two. Same acid. Where does the p H land now?
scenes.caption: Now open the flask. Breathing carries the extra CO₂ away, holding it at 1.2. Same acid. Where does the pH land now?
scenes.narration: Now open the flask. Breathing carries the extra CO₂ away, holding it at 1.2. Same acid. Where does the pH land now?
scenes.visual: Reset to the start: bars back to 24 and 1.2, ratio tag '20 : 1', needle back at 7.40 in the window; the dim 'sealed: about 6.2' needle stays as a faint ghost low on the gauge. On 'open the flask', the GOLD lid lifts off and is replaced by a short tube rising from the top edge to a simple pair of lungs drawn as two rounded outlines (no anatomy detail), labelled 'breathing'. The lungs inflate and deflate slowly from here to the end of the film. On 'Where does the p H land', a question card fills the top third: 'Open flask: where does pH land?' (GOLD, 34), and a GOLD '?' sits beside the needle.
Thinking pause. The question card stays. Nothing changes except slow ambient motion: BLUE water dots drift, the lungs breathe, the needle trembles at 7.40, the ghost needle sits at 6.2.

scenes.tts: About seven point one seven. Bicarbonate falls to fourteen. Carbon dioxide stays put, so the ratio stays near twelve to one. The acid side never builds up.
scenes.caption: About 7.17. Bicarbonate falls to 14. CO₂ stays put, so the ratio stays near twelve to one. The acid side never builds up.
scenes.narration: About 7.17. Bicarbonate falls to 14. CO₂ stays put, so the ratio stays near twelve to one. The acid side never builds up.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. The same ORANGE acid pours in through the funnel ('+10 mM acid'). The PURPLE bar shrinks from 24 to 14 exactly as before (tag '14 mM'). Each new WHITE bubble floats up the tube and out through the lungs on an exhale, so the WHITE bar stays a stub at 1.2 (tag '1.2 mM'). The ratio tag morphs '20 : 1' to '12 : 1' (14 / 1.2 = 11.7). The needle slides from 7.40 down only to 7.17 (6.1 + log10(14/1.2) = 7.167), tag 'open: about 7.17', just below the GOLD window, far above the ghost at 6.2. On 'never builds up', a GOLD arrow traces the bubbles' path out through the lungs.

scenes.tts: That is the trick. Blood's buffer works far from its p K a because blood is not sealed. Breathing carries the extra carbon dioxide away.
scenes.caption: That is the trick. Blood's buffer works far from its pKa because blood is not sealed. Breathing carries the extra CO₂ away.
scenes.narration: That is the trick. Blood's buffer works far from its pKa because blood is not sealed. Breathing carries the extra CO₂ away.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back slightly so the glass, tube, lungs and gauge all fit. The ghost 'sealed' needle at 6.2 and the 'open' needle at 7.17 sit side by side on the gauge; a GOLD bracket between them is labelled 'breathing's rescue'. On 'not sealed', the empty spot where the lid was flashes GOLD. On 'carries the extra', a steady train of WHITE bubbles rises up the tube and leaves with each exhale.

scenes.tts: Real blood does even better. Hemoglobin and other buffers take up part of the acid. Later, the kidneys restore the bicarbonate.
scenes.caption: Real blood does even better. Hemoglobin and other buffers take up part of the acid. Later, the kidneys restore the bicarbonate.
scenes.narration: Real blood does even better. Hemoglobin and other buffers take up part of the acid. Later, the kidneys restore the bicarbonate.
scenes.visual: On 'Hemoglobin and other buffers', a few pale rounded discs with WHITE outlines, labelled 'other buffers', appear in the water and catch some ORANGE proton dots. The needle edges up a little from 7.17 toward the GOLD window, with no number shown (schematic). On 'the kidneys', a small bean-shaped outline at the lower left, labelled 'kidneys', slowly feeds PURPLE slices back into the PURPLE bar until it returns toward 24; the needle settles back in the window at 7.40. The ghost needle fades out.

scenes.tts: Cross much past the window, and proteins change their charges and work less well. The heart rhythm can falter. Less than one p H unit separates ordinary chemistry from emergency.
scenes.caption: Cross much past the window, and proteins change their charges and work less well. The heart rhythm can falter. Less than one pH unit separates ordinary chemistry from emergency.
scenes.narration: Cross much past the window, and proteins change their charges and work less well. The heart rhythm can falter. Less than one pH unit separates ordinary chemistry from emergency.
scenes.visual: The first film's folded ball returns to the middle of the glass, beside the bars, with its GREEN surface beads carrying small '+' and '-' tags and GREEN links between pairs. On 'Cross much past the window', a ghost needle drifts well below the window: ORANGE proton dots settle on several '-' beads, their tags vanish and GREEN links go slack; the ball loosens slightly (schematic). On 'heart rhythm', a small GOLD pulse trace across the top stutters once. On 'Less than one p H unit', a GOLD bracket on the gauge spans less than one unit beside the window, labelled 'under 1 pH unit'. Then the ghost needle fades, protons lift off, links snap back, and the real needle rests in the window.

scenes.tts: A buffer's p K a is not the whole story. Blood's works because each breath throws out the acid side. That helps steady the charges weak bonds need.
scenes.caption: A buffer's pKa is not the whole story. Blood's works because each breath throws out the acid side. That helps steady the charges weak bonds need.
scenes.narration: A buffer's pKa is not the whole story. Blood's works because each breath throws out the acid side. That helps steady the charges weak bonds need.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole world: glass of drifting BLUE water, the PURPLE and WHITE bars at 24 and 1.2, the tube and breathing lungs, the gauge with its needle in the GOLD window, and the folded ball. On 'each breath', one WHITE bubble rises and leaves on an exhale. On 'the charges', the GREEN '+' and '-' tags on the ball glow and their links pulse together once.

END CARD. LINE = 'Blood's buffer works far from its pKa because breathing removes CO₂.' Large GOLD text, centred, over the softly drifting glass of water at 30% opacity, the lungs still slowly breathing behind it.
